title: Of three commerces
paragraphs: We must not rivet ourselves so fast to our humours and temperaments: our chief ability is to know how to apply ourselves to different employments. It is to be, but not to live, to keep oneself tied and bound by necessity to a single course; the bravest souls are those that have in them the most variety and pliancy. Here is an honourable testimony of the elder Cato:
"Huic versatile ingenium sic pariter ad omnia fuit, ut natum ad id unum diceres, quodcumque ageret."
["His gifts were so pliable to every use that you would have said he had been born only for whatever he happened to be doing." — Livy, xxxix. 49.]

If I had the liberty to fashion myself in my own mode, there is no manner so graceful that I would so fix myself to it as not to be able to disengage from it. Life is an unequal, irregular, and multiform motion. It is not to be a friend to oneself, much less a master, but a slave, to be incessantly led by the nose by one's self, and to be so fixed in one's previous inclinations that one cannot turn aside or wrench one's neck out of the collar. I say this now in this part of my life when I find I cannot easily disengage myself from the importunity of my own soul, which cannot ordinarily occupy itself but in things of limited range, nor employ itself except entirely and with all its force. On the lightest subject thrown to it, it expands and stretches itself to that degree that it employs its utmost powers on it; so that idleness is a very painful labour to me, and very damaging to my health. Most men's minds need foreign matter to exercise and enliven them; mine has rather a need of it to sit still and rest:
"Vitia otii negotio discutienda sunt,"
["The vices of idleness must be shaken off by business." — Seneca, Ep. 56.]

— for its chief and hardest study is to study itself. Books are a sort of employment for it that draws it away from that study. With the first thoughts that take possession of it, it begins to bustle and test its vigour in every direction, exercising its powers of handling — now testing its strength, now fortifying, moderating, and arranging itself by way of grace and order. It has of its own enough to rouse its faculties: nature has given it, as it has given everyone else, matter enough of its own to take advantage of, and subjects fit enough on which it may either invent or judge.

Meditation is a strong and full study for those who can effectively taste it and apply themselves to it; I would rather shape my soul than furnish it. There is no employment, either feebler or stronger, than that of entertaining one's own thoughts, depending on what kind of soul one has; the greatest men make it their whole business,
"Quibus vivere est cogitare;"
["For whom to live is to think." — Cicero, Tusc. Quaes., v. 28.]

— nature has therefore favoured it with this privilege, that there is nothing we can do for so long, nor any action we more often and easily give ourselves up to. It is the business of the gods, says Aristotle, and the source of both their beatitude and ours.

The main use of reading, for me, is that by its various objects it rouses my reason and exercises my judgment — not my memory. Few conversations hold me without effort and strain. It is true that beauty and elegance of speech take with me as much as, or more than, the weight and depth of the subject; and since I am apt to be sleepy in all other kinds of talk and give only the rind of my attention, it often happens that in such poor and pitiful conversations — mere chatter — I either make drowsy, unmeaning answers, unbecoming a child and ridiculous, or, more foolishly and rudely still, keep an obstinate silence. I have a pensive way that withdraws me into myself; and along with that, a heavy and childish ignorance of many very ordinary things — by which two qualities I have earned this, that people can truly tell five or six tales as ridiculous about me as about any other man whatever.

But, to proceed with my subject, this difficult constitution of mine makes me very particular about the company I keep with men: I must select and pick them out for my purpose; and it unfits me for common society. We live and have to deal with the public; if their conversation is troublesome to us, if we disdain to apply ourselves to ordinary and vulgar souls (and the ordinary and vulgar are often as regular as those of the finest thread, and all wisdom is folly that does not accommodate itself to the common ignorance), we must give up meddling either with other people's affairs or our own; for business, both public and private, has to do with such people. The least forced and most natural motions of the soul are the finest; the best employments are those least strained. My God, what a good office wisdom does those whose desires it limits to their power! That is the most useful knowledge: "according to what a man can," was Socrates' favourite saying and motto. A motto of great solidity.

We must moderate and adapt our desires to the nearest and easiest things to obtain. Is it not a foolish whim of mine to separate myself from a thousand people to whom my fortune has joined me, and without whom I cannot live, and cleave to one or two who are outside my circle — or rather a fantastic desire for something I cannot obtain? My gentle and easy manners, enemies of all sourness and harshness, may easily enough have saved me from being envied or hated; to be loved, I won't say, but no man ever gave less occasion to be hated. Yet the coldness of my conversation has, reasonably enough, deprived me of the goodwill of many, who may be excused if they interpret it in another and worse sense.

I am very capable of contracting and maintaining rare and exquisite friendships; for since I so greedily seize on the acquaintances that suit my liking, I throw myself with such violence on them that I hardly fail to stick fast and to leave an impression wherever I hit — as I have often happily proven. In ordinary friendships I am somewhat cold and shy, because my motion is not natural when not under full sail. Besides, my fortune having in my youth given me a taste for one sole and perfect friendship, has, in truth, made others somewhat distasteful to me, and stamped too deeply on my mind that friendship is a beast of company, as the ancient said, but not of the herd. I also have a natural difficulty in communicating myself by halves, with the qualifications and the servile, jealous prudence required in the company of numerous and imperfect friendships — and we are mostly thrust onto these in this age of ours, when we cannot talk about the world except either with danger or in falsehood.

Yet I see clearly enough that anyone who has the conveniences of life (I mean the essential conveniences) for his end, as I do, should avoid these difficulties and this delicacy of humour as much as the plague. I would praise a soul of several storeys, that knows both how to stretch itself and to slacken — that finds itself at ease in every condition fortune leads it into; that can talk with a neighbour about his building, his hunting, his quarrels; that can chat with a carpenter or a gardener with pleasure. I envy those who can render themselves familiar with the meanest of their followers and talk with them in their own way; and I dislike Plato's advice, that men should always speak in a magisterial tone to their servants, men or women, without sometimes being playful and familiar; for besides the reasons I have given, it is inhumane and unjust to put such great value on this pitiful prerogative of fortune. The polities where less disparity is permitted between masters and servants seem to me the most equitable. Others study how to raise and elevate their minds; I, how to humble mine and to bring it low; it is only vicious in its expansion:
"Narras et genus AEaci, Et pugnata sacro bella sub Ilio Quo Chium pretio cadum Mercemur, quis aquam temperet ignibus, Quo praebente domum, et quota, Pelignis caream frigoribus, taces."

["You tell us long tales about the race of Aeacus, and the battles fought under sacred Ilium; but what to give for a cask of Chian wine, who will prepare the warm bath, in whose house, and when I may escape the Pelignian cold — that you do not tell us." — Horace, Od., iii. 19, 3.]

Thus, as the Lacedaemonian valour needed moderation, and the sweet and harmonious sound of flutes to soften it in battle, lest they should rush themselves into rashness and fury — whereas other nations commonly use harsh and shrill sounds, and loud and imperious cries, to incite and heat the soldier's courage to the last degree — so too, in my opinion, contrary to the usual method, in the conduct of our minds we have for the most part more need of lead than of wings, of temperance and composure than of ardour and agitation. But, above all, I think it egregiously foolish to put on the grave airs of a man of lofty mind among those who are nothing of the sort: forever to speak in print (as if by the book),
"Favellare in puma di forchetta."
["To talk with the point of a fork," i.e. affectedly.]

You must let yourself down to those you converse with, and sometimes affect ignorance; lay aside power and subtlety in common talk; to preserve decorum and order, that is enough — nay, crawl on the earth, if they so wish.

The learned often stumble at this stone; they will always be parading their pedantic science and strewing their books everywhere; in our day they have so filled the cabinets and the ears of ladies with them that if the ladies have lost the substance, they at least retain the words; so that in any kind of talk, on whatever subject, however mean and common, they speak and write in a new and learned way,
"Hoc sermone pavent, hoc iram, gaudia, curas, Hoc cuncta effundunt animi secreta; quid ultra? Concumbunt docte;"

["In this language they express their fears, their anger, their joys, their cares; in this they pour out all the secrets of their souls; what more? They lie with their lovers learnedly." — Juvenal, vi. 189.]

— and quote Plato and Aquinas on matters the first man they meet could settle as well. The learning that cannot penetrate their souls hangs still upon the tongue. If people of quality would be persuaded by me, they should be content to set out their own proper and natural treasures: they conceal and cover their beauties under others that are not theirs. It is great folly to put out one's own light and shine by a borrowed lustre; they are buried under "de capsula totae" — completely out of their box. It is because they don't sufficiently know themselves or do themselves justice: the world has nothing fairer than them; it's for them to honour the arts and to paint painting itself. What need have they of anything but to live loved and honoured? They have and know but too much for that purpose: they need only rouse and warm a little the faculties they have of their own. When I see them tampering with rhetoric, law, logic, and other such drugs — so improper and unnecessary for their business — I begin to suspect that the men who fill them with such notions do it that they may govern them on that account; for what other excuse can I find? It is enough that, without our instruction, they can compose the graces of their eyes for gaiety, gravity, or sweetness, and season a refusal with sharpness, suspense, or favour; they need no one else to interpret what we say in their service. With this knowledge, they command with a switch, and rule both the tutors and the schools. But if, nevertheless, it angers them to give place to us in anything whatever, and they will out of curiosity have their share in books, poetry is a diversion proper for them: a wanton, subtle, dissembling, prating art, all pleasure and all show, like themselves. They may also extract several commodities from history. From philosophy, out of its moral part, they may select such instructions as will teach them to judge of our humours and conditions, to defend themselves from our treacheries, to regulate the ardour of their own desires, to manage their liberty, to lengthen the pleasures of life, and gently to bear the inconstancy of a lover, the rudeness of a husband, the encroachment of years and wrinkles, and the like. This is the utmost I would allow them in the sciences.

There are some particular natures that are private and retired; my natural way is suited to communication and apt to lay me open. I am all without and in sight, born for society and friendship. The solitude that I love myself and recommend to others is chiefly nothing other than to withdraw my thoughts and affections into myself: to restrain and check, not my steps, but my own cares and desires; resigning all foreign solicitude, and avoiding to death servitude and obligation, and not so much the crowd of men as the crowd of business. Local solitude, to tell the truth, rather gives me more room and sets me more at large; I more readily throw myself onto affairs of state and of the world when I am alone. At the Louvre and in the bustle of the court, I fold myself within my own skin; the crowd pushes me back onto myself; and I never entertain myself so wantonly, with so much licence, or so particularly, as in places of respect and ceremonious caution. Our follies do not make me laugh; it is our wisdom that does. I am not by nature an enemy of court life; I have spent part of mine there, and am of a temperament cheerfully to frequent great company, provided it be at intervals and at my own time. But this delicacy of judgment I'm speaking of perforce ties me to solitude. Even at home, amid a numerous family and in a house frequently visited, I see people enough, but rarely such as I delight to converse with; and I there reserve, both for myself and others, an unusual liberty: there is in my house no such thing as ceremony, ushering, or seeing people down to the coach, and other such troublesome ceremonies as our politeness enjoins (O servile and importunate custom!). Everyone there governs himself by his own method; let whoever wishes speak his thoughts; I sit mute, meditating and shut up in my closet, without any offence to my guests.

The men whose society and familiarity I covet are those they call sincere and able men; and the image of these makes me disrelish the rest. It is, rightly understood, the rarest of our forms, and a form we chiefly owe to nature. The end of this commerce is simply intimacy, frequenting and conferring, the exercise of souls, without any other fruit. In our conversations, all subjects are alike to me; whether there is weight or depth or not, it is all one; there is always grace and pertinency; everything in them is tinted with a mature and constant judgment, and mixed with goodness, freedom, gaiety, and friendship. It is not only in talking of the affairs of kings and state that our wits show their force and beauty, but every bit as much in private conferences. I know my men by their silences and their smiles, and discover them better, perhaps, at table than in council. Hippomachus said very well that he could tell good wrestlers just by seeing them walk in the street. If learning chooses to step into our talk, it shall not be rejected — not magisterial, imperious, and obtrusive, as it commonly is, but subordinate and docile itself: we are there only to pass the time. When we want to be instructed and preached at, we will go look for that on its throne; let it humble itself to us for the moment. For useful and profitable as it is, I imagine we can, when need be, manage well enough without it, and do our business without its help. A well-born soul, practised in the conversation of men, will of herself render herself sufficiently agreeable; art is nothing but the counterpart and register of what such souls produce.
The conversation of beautiful and honourable women is also a sweet commerce to me:
"Nam nos quoque oculos eruditos habemus."
["For we too have eyes that are versed in the matter." — Cicero, Paradox, v. 2.]

If the soul has not so much to enjoy in this commerce as in the first, the bodily senses, which participate more here, bring it to a level next to it — though, in my opinion, not equal to it. But it is a commerce in which one must stand a little on his guard, especially someone like me in whom the body can do much. I scalded myself in my youth at it, and suffered all the torments that poets say befall those who fling themselves into love without order and judgment. It is true that that whipping has made me wiser since:
"Quicumque Argolica de classe Capharea fugit, Semper ab Euboicis vela retorquet aquis."
["Whoever of the Greek fleet escaped the Caphareus rocks ever takes care to steer clear of the Euboean sea." — Ovid, Trist., i. 1, 83.]

It is folly to fix all one's thoughts upon it and engage in it with a furious and indiscreet affection; but on the other hand, to engage there without love and without inclination, like an actor, to play a common part, putting in nothing of one's own but words, is to provide for one's safety, but in as cowardly a way as one who would abandon his honour, profit, or pleasure for fear of danger. For it is certain that from such a practice, those who set it on foot can expect no fruit that can please or satisfy a noble soul. A man must, in good earnest, have desired what he, in good earnest, expects to take pleasure in enjoying; I say this even though fortune should unjustly favour their dissembling — which often happens, because there is no woman, however ugly as the devil, who does not think herself worthy to be loved, and who does not prefer herself before other women, whether for her youth, the colour of her hair, or her graceful walk (for there are no more universally ugly women than there are universally beautiful ones; and such Brahmin virgins as have nothing else to recommend them, the people being assembled by the common crier for the purpose, come out into the marketplace to expose their marriageable parts to public view, to try whether these at least may not be tempting enough to get them a husband). Consequently there is not one of them who does not readily let herself be overcome by the first vow her suitor makes to serve her. Now from this common, everyday treachery of the men of our day, that must follow which we already see by experience: either women rally together and separate themselves off, to avoid us, or else they discipline themselves on the example we give them, play their parts in the farce as we do ours, and give themselves up to the sport without passion, care, or love;
"Neque affectui suo, aut alieno, obnoxiae;"
["Subject neither to their own affections nor to those of others." — Tacitus, Annal., xiii. 45.]

believing, with the persuasion of Lysias in Plato, that they may with more profit and convenience surrender themselves to us the less they love us. Then it will turn out as in comedies, where the audience has as much pleasure as the actors, or more. For my part, I no more acknowledge a Venus without a Cupid than a mother without children: they are things that mutually lend and owe their essence to each other. Thus this cheat recoils on him who is guilty of it; it does not cost him much, indeed, but he also gets little or nothing by it. Those who have made Venus a goddess have noted that her chief beauty was incorporeal and spiritual; but the Venus these people hunt after is not even human, nor indeed brutal — the very beasts will not accept it so coarse and so earthbound. We see that imagination and desire often heat and stir them before the body does; we see in both sexes that, in the herd, they have choice and particular preference in their affections, and that they have among themselves a long commerce of goodwill. Even those whom old age denies the practice of their desire still tremble, whinny, and twitter for love; we see them, before the act, full of hope and ardour; and when the body has played its game, still please themselves with the sweet remembrance of the past delight; some swell with pride after they have performed; others, tired and sated, still express a triumphal joy by their cries. He whose only business is to discharge his body of a natural necessity does not need to trouble others with such elaborate preparations: it is not meat for a gross, coarse appetite.

Since I have no desire that anyone should think me better than I am, I will say this here about the errors of my youth. Not only because of the danger of impairing my health (and yet I could not be so careful but that I had two light mishaps), but also out of a feeling of contempt, I have seldom given myself up to common and mercenary embraces. I would heighten the pleasure by difficulty, by desire, and a certain kind of glory; and I was of Tiberius's mind, who in his amours was as much taken with modesty and birth as with any other quality; and of the courtesan Flora's humour, who never lent herself to less than a dictator, a consul, or a censor, and took pleasure in the dignity of her lovers. Doubtless pearls and gold tissue, titles and train, add something to it.

For the rest, I had a great esteem for wit — provided the person was not objectionable. For, to tell the truth, if one or the other of these two attractions had to be absent, I would rather have lost the understanding part, which has its use in better things; but in the matter of love, a subject mainly concerning the senses of sight and touch, something can be done without the graces of the mind; without the graces of the body, nothing. Beauty is the true prerogative of women, and so peculiarly their own that ours, though it naturally requires a different sort of feature, is never at its best except when youthful and beardless — a sort of confused image of theirs. They say that those who serve the Grand Signior on account of beauty, who are an infinite number, are at the latest dismissed by the age of twenty-two. Reason, prudence, and the offices of friendship are better found among men, and that is why they govern the affairs of the world.

These two engagements are accidental and depend on others; the one is troublesome by its rarity, the other withers with age, so that they could never have been sufficient for the business of my life. That of books, which is the third, is far more certain, and far more our own. It yields the other advantages to the first two, but has the constancy and ease of its service as its own share. It goes step by step with me my whole course, and everywhere it stands by me; it comforts me in old age and in solitude; it eases me of the troublesome burden of idleness, and delivers me at any hour from company I dislike; it blunts the point of griefs, if they are not extreme and have not got total possession of my soul. To divert myself from a troublesome fancy, I have only to run to my books; they at once fix me on them and chase the other out of my thoughts; and they don't mutiny at seeing that I have recourse to them only for want of other, more real, natural, and lively comforts; they always receive me with the same kindness. He may well walk on foot, they say, who leads his horse in his hand; and our James, King of Naples and Sicily, who, handsome, young, and healthy, had himself carried about on a barrow, stretched out on a pitiful mattress, in a poor robe of grey cloth and a cap of the same, yet attended by a royal train, litters, led horses of all sorts, gentlemen and officers — even he represented thereby a tender and unsteady authority: "The sick man has no cause to complain who has his cure in his sleeve." In the experience and practice of this maxim, which is a very true one, lies all the benefit I get from books. In fact, I make no more use of them, so to speak, than those who know them not. I enjoy them as misers do their money, in knowing that I may enjoy them whenever I please; my mind is satisfied with this right of possession. I never travel without books, in peace or in war; and yet sometimes I pass several days, even months, without looking at them. I'll read by and by, I say to myself, or tomorrow, or whenever I please; and meanwhile time slips away without inconvenience. For it is unimaginable how much I please myself and rest content in this thought, that I have them by me to divert myself with whenever I am so disposed, and in remembering what a refreshment they are to my life. It is the best provision I have yet found for this human journey, and I very much pity men of understanding who lack it. I more readily accept any other kind of diversion, however slight, because this one can never fail me.

When at home, I more often visit my library, from which I overlook at once all the concerns of my household. It is situated at the entrance of my house, and I see from there beneath me my garden, courtyard, and back court, and nearly every part of the building. There I turn over now one book, then another, on various subjects, without method or design. Sometimes I meditate; sometimes I record, and dictate as I walk to and fro, such whimsies as these I am setting down for you. It is on the third storey of a tower, of which the ground room is my chapel, the second a chamber with a withdrawing room and closet where I often lie to be more retired; and above is a great wardrobe. This used to be the most useless part of the house. I pass there most of the days of my life, and most of the hours of those days. I am never there at night. Beside it is a cabinet handsome enough, with a fireplace very conveniently contrived, and plenty of light; and were I not more afraid of the trouble than the expense — the trouble that frightens me from all business — I could easily add on either side, on the same floor, a gallery a hundred paces long and twelve wide, having found walls already raised for some other design to the requisite height. Every place of retirement requires a walk: my thoughts go to sleep if I sit still; my fancy doesn't move by itself the way it does when my legs move it; and all those who study without a book are in the same condition. The shape of my study is round, and there is no more open wall than is taken up by my table and chair, so that the rest of the circle presents me a view of all my books at once, ranged on five rows of shelves around me. It has three noble and free prospects, and is sixteen paces across. I am not so continually there in winter, for my house stands on an eminence, as its name implies, and no part of it is so exposed to the wind and weather as this — which pleases me the better, for being of more difficult access and a little remote, both for the sake of exercise and as being there more withdrawn from the crowd. There I am in my kingdom, and there I endeavour to make myself an absolute monarch, and to sequester this one corner from all society — conjugal, filial, and civil. Elsewhere I have only verbal authority, of a confused essence. That man, in my opinion, is very wretched who hasn't somewhere at home where he can be by himself, where he can entertain himself alone, or hide from others. Ambition plagues her converts well enough by keeping them always in show, like the statue in a public square:
"Magna servitus est magna fortuna."
["A great fortune is a great slavery." — Seneca, De Consol. ad Polyb., c. 26.]

They cannot even be private in the water-closet. I have found nothing so severe in the austerity of life that our monks practise as what I have observed in some of their communities — namely, by rule, to have a perpetual society of place, and many persons present at every act whatever; and I think it much more bearable to be always alone than never to be so.

If anyone tells me that it is to undervalue the Muses to use them only for sport and to pass away the time, I shall tell him he does not know as well as I do the value of the sport, the pleasure, and the pastime; I can hardly help adding that any other end is ridiculous. I live from day to day, and, with reverence be it spoken, I live only for myself: there all my designs end. I studied, when young, for show; later, to make myself a little wiser; and now for my diversion — but never for profit. A vain and prodigal humour I once had for this kind of furniture, not just for supplying my own need but for ornament and outward show, I have since quite cured myself of.

Books have many charming qualities for those who know how to choose them; but every good has its ill; it's a pleasure that is not pure and clean, any more than others — it has its drawbacks, and great ones. The soul, it is true, is exercised in it; but the body, the care of which I must on no account neglect, remains meanwhile inactive, and grows heavy and sombre. I know no excess more harmful to me, nor more to be avoided, in this my declining age.
These have been my three favourite and particular occupations; I am not speaking here of those I owe the world by civil obligation.
